```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(knapsack)
set.seed(42)

n <- 2000L
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n, min = 0, max = 10000)
)

median_elapsed <- function(fun, repetitions = 3L) {
  stats::median(replicate(
    repetitions,
    unname(system.time(fun())[["elapsed"]])
  ))
}
```

The 0/1 knapsack problem selects a subset of items with total weight at most
`W` and maximum total value. This report demonstrates the package's brute-force,
dynamic-programming, and greedy functions, then measures the input sizes from
the lab. Timings are measured when the vignette is built, so they reflect the
computer and R version used for that build.

## Brute-force search

Brute force enumerates item subsets and returns an exact result. It is useful
for small inputs and for checking the other algorithms.

```{r brute-force-example}
brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
```

For 16 items there are `2^16 - 1` non-empty subsets. The median elapsed time
below is the answer for this run; the value changes with the computer and R
version.

```{r brute-force-timing}
brute16_seconds <- median_elapsed(function() {
  brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 3500)
})
data.frame(n = 16L, median_elapsed_seconds = brute16_seconds)
```

The exponential number of subsets makes this method unsuitable for large `n`.
The optional parallel extension splits the subset search among workers. The
benchmark below compares sequential and parallel execution on the same 16-item
input. Worker startup has a cost, so parallel execution can be slower for a
small search.

```{r parallel-brute-force}
parallel_items <- knapsack_objects[1:16, ]
sequential_seconds <- unname(system.time(
  sequential_result <- brute_force_knapsack(parallel_items, W = 3500)
)[["elapsed"]])
parallel_seconds <- unname(system.time(
  parallel_result <- brute_force_knapsack(
    parallel_items, W = 3500, parallel = TRUE
  )
)[["elapsed"]])

data.frame(
  mode = c("sequential", "parallel"),
  elapsed_seconds = c(sequential_seconds, parallel_seconds),
  value = c(sequential_result$value, parallel_result$value)
)
```

Both modes should return the same optimum. The measured ratio
`r if (parallel_seconds > 0) sprintf("%.2f", sequential_seconds / parallel_seconds) else "not available"`
is the sequential time divided by the parallel time; a ratio above 1 means
parallel execution was faster on this run.

## Dynamic programming

Dynamic programming is exact for integer weights and integer capacity. Its
time complexity is O(nW). The package implementation updates all capacities
for one item at a time with vectorized operations.

```{r dynamic-example}
knapsack_dynamic(knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
```

For the required case of 500 items and capacity 3,500, the following reports
the median of three elapsed-time measurements.

```{r dynamic-timing}
dynamic_items <- knapsack_objects[1:500, ]
dynamic_seconds <- median_elapsed(function() {
  knapsack_dynamic(dynamic_items, W = 3500)
})
data.frame(n = 500L, W = 3500L, median_elapsed_seconds = dynamic_seconds)
```

### Profiling and optimization

`profvis` can show where the dynamic solver spends time. The chunk profiles
several calls so that the profiler has enough work to display. In this
implementation, the capacity update is vectorized; replacing a capacity loop
with vector operations reduces R-level loop overhead while keeping the same
O(nW) time complexity.

```{r profile-dynamic}
profvis::profvis({
  for (iteration in seq_len(5L)) {
    knapsack_dynamic(dynamic_items, W = 3500)
  }
})
```

The following reference implementation uses a nested R loop over items and
capacities. It is included only to make the optimization comparison
reproducible; the package function remains the vectorized version.

```{r dynamic-reference}
knapsack_dynamic_reference <- function(x, W) {
  n <- nrow(x)
  weights <- x$w
  values <- x$v
  value_table <- matrix(0, nrow = n + 1L, ncol = W + 1L)

  for (item in seq_len(n)) {
    value_table[item + 1L, ] <- value_table[item, ]
    if (weights[item] <= W) {
      for (capacity in seq.int(weights[item], W)) {
        column <- capacity + 1L
        without_item <- value_table[item, column]
        with_item <- value_table[item, capacity - weights[item] + 1L] +
          values[item]
        value_table[item + 1L, column] <- max(without_item, with_item)
      }
    }
  }

  selected <- integer(0)
  remaining <- W
  if (n > 0L) {
    for (item in rev(seq_len(n))) {
      if (value_table[item + 1L, remaining + 1L] !=
          value_table[item, remaining + 1L]) {
        selected <- c(item, selected)
        remaining <- remaining - weights[item]
      }
    }
  }

  list(
    value = round(value_table[n + 1L, W + 1L]),
    elements = selected
  )
}

reference_seconds <- median_elapsed(function() {
  knapsack_dynamic_reference(dynamic_items, W = 3500)
})
vectorized_seconds <- median_elapsed(function() {
  knapsack_dynamic(dynamic_items, W = 3500)
})

data.frame(
  implementation = c("nested-loop reference", "vectorized package function"),
  median_elapsed_seconds = c(reference_seconds, vectorized_seconds)
)
```

On this build, the nested-loop reference took
`r sprintf("%.3f", reference_seconds)` seconds and the vectorized function took
`r sprintf("%.3f", vectorized_seconds)` seconds. The measured speed-up is
`r if (vectorized_seconds > 0) sprintf("%.1f", reference_seconds / vectorized_seconds) else "not available"`x;
it is specific to this machine and should be recalculated on other systems.

## Greedy heuristic

The greedy function sorts items by value-to-weight ratio and takes the
consecutive prefix whose cumulative weight fits. Sorting makes this approach
O(n log n), so it scales to large inputs.

```{r greedy-example}
greedy_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:800, ], W = 3500)
```

The required million-item benchmark is measured below.

```{r greedy-million}
set.seed(42)
large_items <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = 1e6, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(1e6, min = 0, max = 10000)
)
greedy_seconds <- median_elapsed(function() {
  greedy_knapsack(large_items, W = 3500)
})
data.frame(n = 1e6, median_elapsed_seconds = greedy_seconds)
```

This implementation is a heuristic rather than a guaranteed 1/2-approximation:
it does not compare the selected prefix with the best feasible single item.
For example, if the highest-ratio item is too heavy, the prefix can be empty
even when another item fits.

```{r greedy-limitation}
limitation_example <- data.frame(w = c(11, 10), v = c(110, 80))
greedy_knapsack(limitation_example, W = 10)
```

The second item is feasible, but the current prefix rule stops at the first
item and returns an empty selection. This documents a remaining limitation of
the reverted implementation; this report does not change the solver code.

## Summary

Brute force gives an exact answer for small inputs and can distribute work
across workers. Dynamic programming is exact for integer weights and capacity
and runs in O(nW); vectorizing the capacity update reduces interpreter
overhead. The greedy function handles very large inputs quickly, but its
current implementation does not have a formal approximation guarantee. The
timing tables above are recalculated at vignette build time and are not
portable performance promises.
